categories.name: Journal
categories.description: Notes on the work and the seasons from our townhouse workshop in Kitashirakawa. Small records of the days spent making.

tags.name: Seasons
tags.description: Stories of materials and handwork that move with the calendar, gathered through the twenty-four small seasons of the year.

posts.title: New moon letter, October
posts.excerpt: When the ridge of Mount Hiei turns clear, autumn begins in the studio. This month: setting the persimmon dye and getting ready for the November show.

posts.title: Setting persimmon dye
posts.excerpt: Green persimmons, pounded and left in barrels for two years. Dyeing always feels like a letter to your future self.
posts.content:
In October the persimmon tree halfway up the Kitashirakawa slope finally begins to colour. But the fruit we wait for is the other kind: still green, and at its most astringent.

We pound the green fruit in a mortar, pack it into barrels and cover it with water. Left for two years, it becomes amber persimmon tannin. The barrels we filled this year will be ready in the autumn of 2028. Dyeing always feels like writing a letter to your future self.

Seven times over

We dip the linen in tannin and dry it in the sun, then repeat, seven times. After the first dip there is barely any colour. By the third it turns a pale tea brown, and by the seventh a deep red-brown. Sunlight keeps deepening the colour, and use keeps softening the cloth. The work is finished in the hands of whoever uses it.

We do not dye.
We wait for colour.

Yamashina, dyer

This season's persimmon cloth comes in three forms: a door curtain, a wrapping cloth and a book cover. You can see them for the first time at our November exhibition, "The Shape of Ma".

  • Materials: hand-spun Omi linen; green persimmons from Yamashiro, Kyoto
  • Process: two years of fermenting, seven dips, dried in the sun

posts.title: To the Kurotani paper mill
posts.excerpt: In the hills of Ayabe we helped at a paper mill, beginning with stripping the bark from mulberry branches.

posts.title: Opening the kiln
posts.excerpt: Opening a kiln after three days and nights of firing is always a little frightening. We kept nine of twenty-seven bowls.

posts.title: A summer of bamboo
posts.excerpt: We split bamboo dried for three years and carve each pair of chopsticks by knife. The weight that suits a hand is set by the carver.

posts.title: Exhibition: The Shape of Ma
posts.excerpt: From 3 November we open a small exhibition upstairs in the studio: lacquer, paper, cloth, and the work of leaving space.

posts.title: The lacquer room in rain
posts.excerpt: Lacquer cures in humidity. The rainy season is the busiest, and the quietest, time of year for a lacquer artist.

posts.title: Making a book, issue three
posts.excerpt: Work has begun on the third issue of our studio journal, Margin. The theme of this issue is waiting.
